title:
Can you recall, brother, is mother Grogan’s tea and water pot spoken of in the Mabinogion or is it in the Upanishads?
 
 —I doubt it, said Stephen gravely.
 
 —Do you now? Buck Mulligan said in the same tone. Your reasons, pray?
 
 —I fancy, Stephen said as he ate, it did not exist in or out of the Mabinogion. Mother Grogan was, one imagines, a kinswoman of Mary Ann.
html_source:
The Mabinogion is a collection of ancient folklore and considered the earliest prose literature in Britain. While it contains many celtic legends, it is entirely a Welsh rather than Irish text. As well, the Upanishads are a collection of ancient Vedic religious text that contain early theologic concepts of Hinduism. In placing a contemporary Irish character in these texts (Mother Grogan), Mulligan effectively gives Haines the impression that these texts unrelated to Ireland are entirely important and interconnected to the culture, and not regarded with esteem only by theosophists like William Butler Yeats, a prominent Irish poet of the Revivalist movement, whom he mocks earlier.

Furthermore, in recognizing these two texts, one being Britain’s leading colony at the time (India) and the other a nation incorporated into Britain (Wales), Mulligan mocks Haines rather pointedly.

Stephen, however, ends Mulligan’s charade with his own cheeky reply by mentioning that Mother Grogan is related to Mary Ann, a character in another contemporary Irish song.
